paragraphs: At least 17 people have died and 12 others were injured in an explosion at the Habas Demir Celik iron and steel plant in Aliaga, near the western Turkish port city of Izmir, according to the BBC. Al Jazeera reported a toll of at least 16 dead and 13 injured. The BBC said President Recep Tayyip Erdogan first gave the toll as 16, and that Health Minister Kemal Memisoglu later announced that a critically injured person had died.

The blast happened on Monday, at 11:46am local time according to Al Jazeera. Izmir Governor Suleyman Elban said it followed the collapse of a crane carrying a replacement boiler, which caused materials to fall into a furnace below. The company said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces. The governor said some people were believed to still be under the rubble, and Izmir Mayor Cemil Tugay said the full number of dead and injured would only be clear once the rubble was cleared.

After a cabinet meeting, Erdogan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way while search and rescue work continued. The BBC, citing its Turkish service and local media, reported that at least five people have been arrested.

Workers' groups point to a history of safety problems. The Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey. The Izmir chapter of the Labour Party, a small Marxist group, said this was the third fatal incident at the factory in three weeks, and said seven employees had died in accidents there over ten years. It said maintenance requirements and safety standards were not being met. The company's response to those claims was not reported in the pages. The European Union and Azerbaijan were among those who sent condolences.

British comedian Russell Brand, 51, was sentenced on Monday to ten years and six months in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, according to The Guardian and NPR. Judge Bennathan handed down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court, and his remarks were broadcast live.

A jury convicted Brand last week after a four-week trial. The offences were committed between 2004 and 2009 and involved a woman at a bar, a radio station worker, a TV studio worker and a 21-year-old fan who was raped at his London home in 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault. Brand denies all charges and has said he never had non-consensual sex, NPR reported.

The judge said Brand had told the trial a series of lies and had shown a casual, arrogant disregard of any woman's right to say no. He also paid tribute to the bravery of the women who gave evidence. Four of the women gave victim impact statements. One said she carries the trauma every day, and another said hearing his voice on television has made her jump.

Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, told the court Brand was a fundamentally different person today and was not, in general terms, a rapist. He described Brand as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given. Six people submitted character references. The prosecution had asked for a long sentence, citing aggravating factors in the rape case.
The Guardian reported that the Metropolitan Police said, after the convictions, that Brand is under investigation over two further rape allegations.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell told the opening session of the COP31 climate talks in Turkey on Monday that a global fossil fuel price crisis is spreading inflation like a cancer, according to The Guardian. He said this fossil fuel cost chaos had delivered a global shock wave that hit households hard. The Guardian reported that the war with Iran and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz oil route pushed petrol prices up by 50% around the world, raising inflation and slowing economic growth.

Delegates from almost 200 countries are attending the two-week talks in Antalya. Turkey expects 100,000 visitors, including at least 95 heads of state, with a leaders summit on Wednesday and Thursday. Turkey is hosting, and Australia, whose climate minister Chris Bowen is president of the negotiations, is leading them. The two are promoting a voluntary goal to raise electricity's share of final energy consumption from about one-fifth to one-third within ten years. Bowen said there was enormous momentum for the idea, and International Energy Agency head Fatih Birol said it would send an unmistakable signal to markets if endorsed.

The talks open under pressure. The Guardian said climate scientists confirmed this year that global heating would reach at least 1.8C, beyond the 1.5C Paris goal. Bowen said the target would be overshot but that the world can return to it. A 20-member high-ambition coalition says the 1.5C limit cannot be abandoned and is pressing for faster finance for vulnerable countries. The Marshall Islands' Jess Gasper said it took eight years to secure funding for a single sea wall.
The agenda was agreed without a fight, which many saw as a good sign. Delegates expect the final decision to refer to the electrification goal.

Geothermal company Fervo said in its third-quarter earnings report on Monday that it has $11.9 billion in contracted revenue, up from $7.2 billion last quarter, according to TechCrunch. The company is on track to finish a 396 megawatt plant for Google by the end of 2028, and it connected its first 100 megawatt plant to the grid earlier this year. Both are at Cape Station in Utah, a resource now thought to be able to generate 8.4 gigawatts, against the roughly 4 gigawatts experts had earlier suggested.

CEO Tim Latimer said the Google project, now called Cape Google 400, will be grid connected, so Google can draw power and sell it to others if it is not ready to use it. Fervo builds in phases. Its newer wells are deeper and hotter, each capable of 15 megawatts gross, and several are linked into units it calls GeoBlocks. The first generated 33 megawatts and recent ones reached 50 megawatts.

The business is still early. Fervo ended the quarter with an operating loss of $43.7 million, with $1.9 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $301.6 million in long-term debt. TechCrunch said much depends on lowering costs. The first phase of Cape Station cost $7,000 per kilowatt of capacity, and the Google project costs $5,500. With subsidies, TechCrunch said, that is roughly comparable to a new gas plant burning fuel at $6 per million BTUs, about twice today's price. Fervo's long-term target is $3,000 per kilowatt.

Separately, TechCrunch reported that Anthropic is spending $3.4 billion on Caterpillar gas turbines capable of up to 1.7 gigawatts, citing a Financial Times report. It noted that turbine backlogs stretch into the early 2030s.

Pope Leo XIV met five survivors of clerical sexual abuse in Buenos Aires on Monday, the second day of his visit to Argentina, according to Al Jazeera. The Vatican said the private meetings were the first of several he plans with survivors during his 12-day Latin America tour. The Vatican said the pope spoke with each person individually and listened to their painful stories and to their proposals for strengthening paths toward healing within the Church.

The meetings followed an open-air Mass that drew an estimated 2.5 million people to Avenida del Libertador, a major boulevard in the capital. Al Jazeera described it as the country's first papal liturgy in nearly 40 years. The visit is the first by a pontiff since Pope John Paul II's trip in 1987.

The survivors' meeting lasted more than an hour. Leo, 71, reiterated his pledge to strengthen safeguarding in the Catholic Church. The Holy See Press Office said in October that such meetings reflect his wish to express closeness to those who have suffered and to make the Church a safe and spiritually healthy place.

Al Jazeera said Leo, the first pope born in the United States, has consistently met survivors on foreign trips as part of a wider effort to repair relations and restore the Church's credibility after three decades of lawsuits, widespread abuse and cover-ups. Before becoming pope, he served as president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America.
Argentina is the second stop on a three-country tour that began in Uruguay and ends in Peru.

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban has accused the country's new government of political persecution after the reported arrest of his younger brother, Aron Orban, according to Al Jazeera. Police arrested Aron Orban on Monday on suspicion of people smuggling, among other offences, according to a press report shared by Prime Minister Peter Magyar.

The news was first reported by Kontroll, a site owned by Magyar's brother, Marton. Local media reported that police raided properties linked to Aron Orban's business associates but did not confirm whether he was among those detained. Authorities said they had detained four people suspected of people smuggling.

Viktor Orban said on X that the government arrested his brother to divert attention from other issues. He wrote that he is the real target and that his brother is simply being used to get to him. The government's response to that claim was not given in the report.

Aron Orban built several successful businesses during his brother's 16 years in power, as other members of the family did. Last year, an investigation by the news site Telex linked him and his business associates to an alleged scheme involving visas for foreign guest workers. Viktor Orban's strong opposition to immigration defined his time in office.

Magyar, a pro-EU conservative, won a landslide victory in April and had promised to investigate his predecessor's alleged corruption and abuse of power while in office. What charges, if any, Aron Orban will face has not been reported.

Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders have agreed to open two new border crossings, coordinate emergency responses and share archival materials, as part of a United Nations-backed effort to restart peace talks, according to Al Jazeera. Greek Cypriot leader Nikos Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman met UN special envoy Maria Angela Holguin on Monday in the UN-controlled buffer zone. Al Jazeera called it the first concrete sign of detente after nearly a decade of deadlock.

The UN described the meeting as positive and said the leaders would talk again in the coming weeks in the presence of outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. Christodoulides said the single goal was resuming talks before the end of Guterres's term at the end of the year. Media in Cyprus said the move would bring the number of open crossings to 11.
Guterres began a new push in the summer, suggesting that new crossings could build trust. The two sides have since disagreed over ground rules for talks.

Cyprus was split in 1974 when Turkey invaded and seized the north in response to a coup instigated by the then-military government in Greece. A power-sharing administration had collapsed in 1963, and a UN peacekeeping force has monitored a 180km ceasefire line since. Only Turkey recognises the north as an independent republic, and Ankara keeps more than 35,000 troops there.

Decades of talks have failed to reunify the island, and the last official round collapsed in 2017. Greek Cypriots oppose any hands-on Turkish involvement, while Turkish Cypriots say it is essential. Last year the north elected its first pro-unification leader since 2020.

South African police have arrested nine Zimbabweans who were allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and Ukraine, according to the BBC. Al Jazeera, which did not state the suspects' nationalities, also reported the arrests. The group, aged 20 to 26, was detained on Sunday evening by a multidisciplinary team that included Interpol. Five were arrested at OR Tambo airport and four at a hotel in Bruma, near Johannesburg, as they prepared to board flights, police said.

They are charged under the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which outlaws mercenary activity without government permission. The BBC said all nine later appeared in court, while Al Jazeera said a court date had not been given. The reports differ on destination: Al Jazeera said they were heading to Russia, while the BBC said their final destination was unclear and that police had not said which side they meant to fight for or named any organisations that arranged their travel.

Both outlets describe a wider pattern. Al Jazeera cited a September report by Amnesty International accusing Russia of tricking foreigners into fighting in what it called human trafficking. A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated that more than 1,700 people from 36 African countries have been recruited to fight for Russia. Kenya estimated that 252 of its citizens were illegally conscripted, and Zimbabwe said in March that 15 of its nationals had been killed.

South Africa said it secured the return of 17 South Africans allegedly tricked into joining the war, according to the BBC, though Al Jazeera gave the figure as 11. The BBC added that Ukraine has also recruited foreign nationals, including from Africa.

Sen. Dan Sullivan's re-election campaign filed a motion on Monday to intervene in a lawsuit brought by Democrat Mary Peltola's Senate campaign against the Alaska Division of Elections. Peltola's campaign sued on Friday, seeking access to records for absentee ballots that were preliminarily rejected in the midterm election, according to Fox News.

Sullivan's campaign argued that the lawsuit seeks to force elections officials to ignore state law. Campaign spokesman Nate Adams called it an attempt to "rig the system" in Peltola's favor and said it was "further evidence that she is not confident she can win on the merits alone." Adams also said Sullivan's campaign is following Alaska precedent to make sure every legally cast ballot is counted, and that it remains confident Sullivan will win once all ballots are counted. The Fox News report did not include a response from Peltola's campaign to the motion.

The Division of Elections responded to the lawsuit by saying individual voters have not yet been notified that their ballots were rejected. It said it would be improper to give Peltola's campaign access to that data before the voters themselves.
The race remains extremely close. As of Monday, Peltola led Sullivan by just over 600 votes, with more than 25% of votes still to be counted, Fox News reported.

The dispute sits alongside a separate fight over what Sullivan and Republicans call a "Decoy Dan" scheme, in which an independent named Daniel J. Sullivan appeared on the ballot. Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said the Division of Elections initially found the candidacy illegitimate and kept him off the ballot, but the state Supreme Court ruled against the Division. After a New York Times report tied potential knowledge of the scheme to Peltola's campaign, Dunleavy reopened the investigation. Fox News also linked to coverage in which Peltola said she knew nothing about it.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in West Texas, granting an emergency request from the federal government, according to Fox News. The ruling stays a preliminary injunction issued last month by a federal district judge in El Paso, who had temporarily halted construction in the area U.S. Customs and Border Protection designates as the Big Bend Sector while the litigation continues.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated she would have denied the stay request but did not file a written dissent.

The lawsuit was brought by a coalition of environmental groups and local residents. They claim the Department of Homeland Security violated constitutional provisions by proceeding without congressional authorization and by bypassing environmental regulations. The case remains pending, and the Supreme Court's action addresses only the lower court's hold on construction.

The Big Bend Sector spans more than 500 miles and covers roughly a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border. Reuters reported it accounted for just 1.3% of all border apprehensions in 2025. Administration officials have argued the wall is vital to stopping cartel operations south of the border and curbing the smuggling of large quantities of illicit drugs. They say most of the proposed construction will occur on privately owned land.

Big Bend National Park is slated for a 17-mile barrier, though officials noted it will not use the 30-foot steel pedestrian fencing planned elsewhere along the southern border. Fox News also reported that Mullin told Congress the primary border wall will be done by June 2027 and the secondary wall by summer 2028. President Donald Trump has long promoted wall expansion as a signature part of his border strategy.

A Utah judge ruled on Monday that Tyler Robinson, 23, will stand trial in early July 2028 for the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Judge Tony Graf set jury selection to begin June 21, 2028, with 105 days reserved for the trial, which will remain in Provo. Robinson has pleaded not guilty.

The date falls between the competing proposals. According to the Washington Examiner, prosecutors had asked for a start on Jan. 31, 2028, while Robinson's lawyers sought the third quarter of 2029, arguing they need years to prepare given the amount of evidence. Lawyers for Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, asked for a start by Oct. 4, 2027, and asserted her right to a speedy trial. The Guardian reported that the defense had asked for January 2029 and Erika Kirk for October 2027.

Graf said starting in under a year could put the trial or jury deliberations over Christmas 2027, and that "unnecessary delay remains a serious concern." President Donald Trump had written last month that the case should be tried within a month and that the judge was "desecrating the memory of the Great Charlie Kirk."

Robinson faces five charges, including aggravated murder, and could face the death penalty if convicted. Prosecutors allege he shot Kirk from a rooftop at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, and say he held grievances over Kirk's political views. At a July hearing, the court watched a video in which Robinson's former roommate said Robinson expressed regret. Defense attorneys questioned the motive theory and the reliability of forensic evidence, including DNA found on a towel wrapped around a firearm. The Examiner noted the trial will unfold during the 2028 presidential election season.

A Massachusetts judge ruled on Monday that Lindsay Clancy can be tried again on murder charges, rejecting her attorneys' bid to dismiss the case. Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth said a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject her to double jeopardy. He declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after jurors reported that a holdout juror was preventing a unanimous verdict.

Clancy is accused of strangling her three children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, with exercise bands at their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. According to The Guardian, no one at the first trial disputed that she did so. Her lawyers argue she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should be found not guilty by reason of insanity. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional, the BBC reported. Some jurors later said in televised interviews that, but for one holdout, they were prepared to reach that verdict. A first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life without parole.

The defense argued that Sullivan acted prematurely and should have questioned the holdout juror and possibly removed that person. Prosecutors under District Attorney Timothy Cruz countered that questioning the holdout could have meant improper interference in deliberations.

In his ruling, Sullivan wrote that a mistrial is "not to be avoided by intrusion into the jury's domain" and found there was "manifest necessity" for it. He also denied a defense request for the holdout juror's records and to question that juror under oath, calling it "impermissibly coercive." A hearing on Nov. 16 will discuss scheduling a second trial, which the judge has suggested could begin in March. The BBC said prosecutors could reduce the charges or dismiss them.

Federal safety regulators have opened a new investigation into whether Waymo's fix for robotaxis illegally passing stopped school buses actually worked. In a November 6 filing, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said a majority of the reported incidents happened after Waymo deployed a software update meant to solve the problem. Reuters first reported the filing, according to TechCrunch.

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened a "recall query" to "assess the adequacy of the remedy." Waymo said last year that the update was completed for all affected vehicles on November 17, 2025. Wired reported that an official voluntary recall followed about a month later. Passing a stopped school bus with its lights flashing and stop arm out is illegal in all 50 states.

The original investigation began in October 2025 after footage showed a Waymo vehicle maneuvering around a stopped school bus in Atlanta that was unloading children. Further incidents were documented in Austin, where Austin Independent School District officials reported at least five, according to a letter filed with NHTSA. Wired reported that the National Transportation Safety Board, which is also investigating, found another incident in mid-January. It added that the Austin district helped Waymo hold a data collection event with school buses and stop signals after the recall, yet incidents continued.

Waymo said it has made "significant improvements" and has received no citations since March 2026. A spokesperson said the company will respond to NHTSA's query once it is received. Wired noted that recall queries like this one have in past years led to civil penalties costing companies tens of millions of dollars.

Anthropic on Monday released two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, as the company prepares for a potentially historic IPO that CNBC said could happen as soon as next week. Fable 5.2 is generally available now, while Mythos 5.2 is open only to vetted organizations through the company's Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Anthropic said the models generate outputs 30% faster than their predecessors and cost 20% less than the 5.1 generation, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. The company claims improvements in coding, reasoning and vision. According to The Verge, Anthropic said that in prerelease testing the models helped engineers complete software migrations, designed three working electronic devices, solved two open problems in black hole physics and formalized a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours. These are the company's own claims.

CNBC reported it is the first release of Anthropic frontier models since CEO Dario Amodei called in September for slowing the pace of AI development. Dianne Penn, the company's head of product management for research, said, "We called for pacing, not pausing." Anthropic said the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing.

Penn said Fable 5.2 is aimed at power users and hard problems in engineering, mathematics and robotics, while models like Claude Opus 5.5 suit daily tasks. On the IPO, CNBC reported Anthropic is aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a $2 trillion target floated earlier. Its amended prospectus shows $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from a year earlier. Executives must still persuade investors during the roadshow that the company's approach to balancing safety and competition is right.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release the October consumer price index on Tuesday at 8:30 a.m. Economists in the Dow Jones consensus forecast expect headline prices to rise 0.3% and core prices, which exclude food and energy, to rise 0.2%. Both would be slower than September's monthly gains of 0.6% and 0.3%, CNBC reported.

Gasoline prices fell more than 4% in October, according to the Energy Information Administration. Even so, Federal Reserve officials say they are worried that inflation first pushed up by tariffs and the Iran war is proving more persistent than expected and spreading into other sectors. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday that inflation is now rising in areas like services that probably were not tied to oil or tariffs. He said the AI data center build-out is starting to look like "old-fashioned demand overheating."

There will be no annual reading for October because last year's government shutdown prevented the BLS from collecting some data. Bank of America, using an interpolated baseline, estimated annual growth of 3.8% for headline and 2.7% for core inflation, each 0.1 point higher than September.

The backdrop is strong. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter, payrolls rose 165,000 in October, and unemployment fell to 4.1%, though inflation-adjusted wage growth has been negative. The Fed held rates in October, but CME FedWatch data show markets pricing better than an 80% chance of a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting. Bank of America economist Stephen Juneau said this is the last inflation report before that meeting and that only an "indisputably soft" 0.1% reading would likely dissuade a hike. He said the bigger risk to the call comes from financial markets.

Nonfarm payrolls grew by 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, far above the 59,000 economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast. CNBC pointed to three less-noticed parts of the report that helped explain the surge.

The first was consulting. Employment for management, scientific and technical consultants rose 17,300 between September and October, the largest monthly increase in nearly two years, and pushed the group past 1.9 million workers for the first time on record. Some economists speculate businesses are hiring consultants to help adopt AI. Moody's Analytics found AI has created a net 786,000 jobs since ChatGPT launched in November 2022, partly through data center construction. Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi wrote that the risk of AI job losses has not gone away, but that for now AI is adding to job growth.

The second was temporary hiring, which grew by 18,600, one of its largest monthly gains since 2022. Economists often treat temp hiring as a leading indicator, since short-term workers can be moved into full-time roles. CNBC noted, however, that early holiday hiring could also explain the boost, in which case those workers might not be retained in January. Couriers and messengers made up just over one in 10 new jobs.

The third was election spending. Employment in political organizations has historically peaked in October of midterm and presidential years, according to a BLS analysis. OpenSecrets said the 2026 midterm is on track to be the most expensive on record, which may have created more paid campaign work than usual. Analysts quoted said the consulting sector is worth watching and the courier category bears watching for a reversal.

Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon told CNBC on Monday that financing demand for AI infrastructure remains strong despite recent market jitters. He said his firm has been "very active" in AI capital markets deals in recent weeks and expects that to continue. "There's still very strong demand for investments in the AI infrastructure build," he said.

AI-related stocks, including chipmakers and neocloud providers, have fallen in recent weeks as investors question whether the hundreds of billions of dollars going into AI infrastructure will pay off. CNBC reported the selloff began before the midterm elections and intensified after Democrats won sweeping victories on Tuesday, raising concerns that political opposition could slow the industry's expansion. Solomon said changes in the political environment will "create recalibrations and ups and downs," but that he still believes deeply in AI's long-term power to drive productivity.

He also pushed back on political resistance to data center construction, arguing the infrastructure is essential to the U.S. economy and can be built responsibly. If it is not built in the U.S., he said, it will naturally go elsewhere because the demand for compute exists.
Goldman is among the banks leading Anthropic's potential IPO. Solomon declined to comment in detail but said the market environment is "still pretty constructive."

Separately, Bloomberg reported that banks led by JPMorgan could offer one of the year's biggest discounts to sell part of $5 billion in debt for software firm Qualtrics that underwriters were stuck holding. According to people with knowledge of the matter, nearly $2 billion would be marketed in the high-yield bond market, at a coupon of at least 8% and a price of about 85 cents on the dollar. Investor meetings are scheduled this week.

Neocloud companies, which rent out AI computing power, have seen their stock prices cut in half over the past month. Investors are now waiting to hear how the leaders plan to handle tighter credit and an unfavorable political climate. CoreWeave reports quarterly results on Tuesday and Nebius on Thursday, CNBC reported. Both rely on debt to buy advanced AI systems.

Last Thursday the neoclouds fell sharply, contributing to the Nasdaq's steepest slump in 19 months. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Micron also dropped on worries that anti-AI sentiment would complicate buildout plans. Democrats won governors' races in five states last week, and voters rejected data centers in all but one of 41 related ballot measures. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator wrote on LinkedIn that the company does not expect any impact to customer commitments or backlog from the political shifts.

Credit markets were less reassured. Yields on some CoreWeave bonds maturing in 2031 rose above 16%, and the spread on its five-year credit default swaps topped 1,240 basis points, up 50% in a month. At the end of June, CoreWeave had $5.5 billion in cash and $35 billion in debt. Morningstar analyst Luke Yang said a near-term bankruptcy is unlikely and the company can deliver on existing contracts, but growth will require more capital, and a depressed stock makes equity raising hard. Paul Meeks of Freedom Capital Markets called the situation a "doom cycle" but said he expects some relief from earnings.

Analysts expect CoreWeave's revenue to grow about 160% to $3.55 billion and Nebius's to grow sixfold to about $908 million. IREN's stock jumped 20% Friday after it reported AI cloud revenue more than doubled.

President Donald Trump said Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told him he had "no idea she was a spy" when he had an affair with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe worked for Beijing. "I really believe him," Trump told reporters, according to the BBC. He said the FBI was also investigating but did not elaborate or say when that probe began. A day earlier, Trump had said he had not spoken to Huang about the matter.

Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation after reports that Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort," the company said in a Sunday statement. In an email to staff, Huang wrote, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did." Nvidia said it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised. According to The New York Times and the Financial Times, US intelligence agencies say Alice Huang, an executive at the cloud company Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing.

China has rejected the claims. Its foreign ministry told reporters the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China," according to the BBC. Spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" unsubstantiated, Reuters reported.

Nvidia's stock closed 4.27% lower Monday, CNBC reported. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. said any talk of replacing Huang was "comedy," but added that the board investigation creates "huge uncertainty" for investors. Trump had earlier called Huang "an honorable guy."
Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.

Jensen Huang's admission of an affair with a woman US intelligence officials believe was a Chinese spy has raised questions about what would happen to Nvidia if its 63-year-old co-founder were forced out, CNBC reported. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% Monday even as the broader market rallied. The company says Huang will keep leading it during the board's investigation, and the board said it has "confidence in Jensen" and "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised." China has called the spy allegation a smear.

Analysts say the company has no obvious successor. "The issue at Nvidia is that there is no clear successor to Jensen, and we had expected him to stay in this role for at least 10 more years," analysts at Melius Research wrote. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon said, "Jensen is Nvidia. Nvidia is Jensen," adding that Huang "runs the thing pretty much top down." Huang is also president, and CNBC said internal records show he had 33 direct reports this week.

Huang owns just over 3% of Nvidia's shares and is one of 11 board members on a board with no official chair, according to CNBC. Nvidia's filings do not name him as a key person, instead citing dependence on its "longstanding executive team."

Timm Schulze-Melander of Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote that Huang could be forced to step back if the investigation finds "something materially more serious" than an undisclosed relationship, but said resignation is not a foregone conclusion. Several analysts said the probe could lead to governance changes, including a contingency plan for a transition. Melius said the company has a "strong bench" of executives, but that "Jensen is one of a kind."

Political pressure is also building. Leaders from both parties are calling for briefings, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote that Democrats poised to take control of Congress want investigations and new legislation on advanced AI chips and China. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, has come under international attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted being unfaithful to his wife, following reports linking him to Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. According to The New York Times, US intelligence officials believe she is a Chinese intelligence asset. Jensen Huang did not name her or the company in his statement, which said Nvidia's board had begun an independent investigation into "the national security concerns raised in news reports."

Megaspeed sells Asia Pacific companies access to computing power hosted in Southeast Asian data centers, and advertises itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia's cloud business in the region. CNBC noted that US controls restrict exports of some advanced chips to China, but remote access to chips located elsewhere is a separate question. A Bloomberg report in December 2025 said the US government was investigating Megaspeed's ownership and whether it smuggled Nvidia chips to China. Megaspeed responded on its website that the report contained "misleading information and incorrect insinuations," saying inspections by US, Malaysian and Nvidia officials found "no evidence of any violations."

A House Select Committee on China statement on Nov. 5 called Alice Huang a "publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset." The committee has asked Jensen Huang to attend a Nov. 18 briefing. The Times reported she is a Chinese citizen well-connected among chip executives, and that a memo circulated in the Trump administration last spring described a Chinese businesswoman close to Huang passing information on US AI chips to Beijing. Bloomberg reports she also goes by Huang Le and helped set up Megaspeed in 2023. Singapore's government said it had not investigated her alleged intelligence ties or her relationship with Huang.

CNBC said it had contacted Megaspeed for comment. Nvidia said its board's inquiry would "examine all available information" and that it has no reason to believe secrets or national security were compromised.

President Donald Trump signaled Monday that he considers the US-Israeli war against Iran "effectively" over, after meeting Qatari mediators, Al Jazeera reported. At a surprise briefing, he repeated his position that the US had destroyed Iran's military. "Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We're just keeping it the status quo," he said, adding that he was doing so "at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."

Trump said the status quo means continuing the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, along with the newly announced Task Force Iron Gate, which aims to cut off trade by land and through the Caspian Sea. He said Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others would prefer to keep things as they are. The remarks followed a White House meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, hosted by Trump and Vice President JD Vance. The prime minister posted that he was grateful for "positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region."

Al Jazeera said it was unclear whether the comments change US posture significantly. Trump declined to commit to a long-term ceasefire. "I don't guarantee anything," he said. "But if we do have to go back in, we are locked and loaded and ready to go."

Iranian officials dismissed the remarks. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, wrote on social media that Washington was "manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks." Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, speaking through the state-aligned Tasnim news agency, said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had called for an end to a situation he described as "neither war nor peace." Pezeshkian said Iran was open to negotiations but would not be coerced. Both sides have claimed victory throughout the conflict.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky on Monday reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, forcing a House vote within two legislative days, meaning Wednesday at the latest, according to Fox News. The resolution lists eight charges, including three for waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution, others over strikes on alleged drug boats, the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization, and the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly over a video about illegal orders. "Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Massie said, according to the BBC.

Hegseth called the effort "sham articles of impeachment" in a video, saying, "Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me." Trump said Monday, "I'll stand by him." Massie, who lost his primary to a candidate Hegseth campaigned for, said Democrats would be "very vicious" when they take charge. Hegseth plans a news conference Tuesday.

Whether the measure passes is disputed. Fox News reported several House Republicans privately think it could, citing absences of members who lost elections and negative sentiment toward Hegseth, though most Republicans are expected to oppose it. Leaders could also move to table it or refer it to committee. Peter Loge of George Washington University told the BBC it was "likely to pass the House because the Republican majority is so slim." Massie said he was not sure it had enough backing. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he is a "hard yes."

Rep. Warren Davidson, an Ohio Republican who criticizes the war, opposes impeachment, calling it an effort to scapegoat Hegseth and saying administrations back to the Korean War have largely ignored Congress's war powers. Conviction in the Senate requires two-thirds, which NPR said is unlikely.

France has formally accused Iran of carrying out a series of destructive cyberattacks last month that took over refrigeration systems at about 700 retail sites. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said, "I am able to confirm that the Islamic Republic of Iran's Revolutionary Guards are responsible," and called the campaign "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression." He said Europe-wide sanctions would follow and that Iran's ambassador had been summoned.

According to the French cybersecurity agency ANSSI, hackers linked to Iran's military raised temperatures in supermarkets and butcher shops overnight on Oct. 11 and 12, spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food. The Guardian reported temperatures rose from as low as -27C to above 50C, thousands of tons of food were dumped, and in some stores the heat sparked fires. Several small hydroelectric plants were also targeted, with what ANSSI called "moderate effects."

Paris Prosecutor Laure Beccuau said investigators identified a modus operandi of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit linked to the Revolutionary Guards, citing Farsi and IP addresses traced to devices in Iran. Her office opened an investigation into the unit's head and deputies and is requesting international arrest warrants.

Similar incidents followed. Last week hackers accessed cold stores holding blood products at a French blood bank, though technicians disconnected them before products were destroyed, and retailers in 11 European countries reported refrigeration problems. The Guardian noted it is not clear whether those incidents are linked. NPR said the attacks fit a wider 2026 trend that has hit Europe, Israel and the United States, and that France is the first government to formally assign blame. US officials suspect Iran in earlier incidents, but the Pentagon has made no official statement.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said ministers will discuss the matter at next Monday's foreign affairs council. Iran's response was not included in the articles.

President Donald Trump questioned the honesty of last week's midterm elections in a Monday post on Truth Social, days after saying he would accept the results. "Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???" he wrote. He made vague references to polling, ballot "dumps" and "machines" without providing evidence of error or wrongdoing, the BBC and Al Jazeera reported.

The post appeared to contradict what Trump told The New York Times on election night, that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results. He also congratulated Democrats on a call with CBS News and told Fox News the party "did a good job." Democrats retook both chambers of Congress. As of now they hold 54 Senate seats and 254 House seats, with counting continuing in places such as Alaska and Mississippi, the BBC said.

State and local officials said voting had been mostly problem-free. MIT political scientist Charles Stewart III said election-night vote reporting followed standard patterns. Ruth Greenwood of Harvard's Election Law Clinic said slower counts in some states do not mean "anything nefarious is occurring." Al Jazeera cited a Pew Research analysis finding pre-election polls understated the Democratic margin by at least 2 points in 23 of 27 governor and Senate races.

Trump has previously attributed the loss partly to the Iran war and gasoline prices, and told CBS, "We would have won easily if I was on the ballot." The BBC noted that courts rejected challenges to the 2020 election and that judges ruled against nearly all Justice Department lawsuits over vote counts in states including California and Alaska.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Trump's "return to election denialism was inevitable." Commentator Megyn Kelly replied on X, "Just stop." The White House's response was not reported in the articles.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries did not confirm Monday that he has the votes to become speaker, even as he said he was confident. "We have a vote next Wednesday," he told reporters. When a reporter said he sounded as if he lacked the 218 votes needed, Jeffries replied, "I guess we'll find out," and later said, "We're very confident we'll get there." The Washington Examiner reported that a group of new progressive members, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, have not ruled out forcing a recorded vote in the caucus's internal race, which is normally a secret ballot.

Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy of New Jersey said the group is "not withholding votes" but is undecided and wants a conversation about "what's the plan going forward." The outlet noted that no other candidates have been floated and that Democrats hold a majority of more than 250 seats, giving Jeffries room to lose a few votes.

Republicans are also dealing with leadership questions. Fox News reported that Senate Republicans are slated to hold leadership elections Tuesday, with Majority Leader John Thune expected to seek another term. Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin wrote to conference chair Tom Cotton asking to delay the vote so members can discuss a path forward after what he called a "stunning defeat." Party rules allow a delay if five senators sign, and Johnson says he has them, including Rick Scott, John Kennedy, Ted Budd and Mike Lee. Sens. David McCormick and Jim Banks, who did not sign, also want a pause.

A GOP aide told Fox that part of Thune's popularity is his willingness to take feedback. Thune is expected to run unopposed, and Scott said he does not want to run, though he said "we'll see" whether he supports Thune. The Fox page did not report the House Republican side of the delay question.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday that President Trump has encouraged him to work with Democrats who have reached out about immigration reform, but that enforcement policies are not changing, Fox News reported. Speaking to reporters at a counter-drone conference in Maryland, Mullin said "a lot of Democrats" had contacted him. "The president has said, 'Let's start working with them and then let's meet at some point,'" he said. Asked whether policy changes had been discussed, he said, "No, we haven't had that conversation," and added, "We're never going to allow amnesty to happen."

Mullin also suggested Congress could consider a path to permanent legal status for recipients of the DACA program, saying it would "be up to Congress." Fox described this as his first public suggestion of that kind and a shift in tone from a March DHS post stressing that DACA "does not confer any form of legal status." Fox noted the comments came as Trump named Stephen Miller, architect of his hardline immigration policies, as White House chief of staff, and said the White House has doubled down after the president angered some of his base by floating a deal with Democrats. DHS did not respond to a request for comment.

Democrats set out a different position. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Monday that Democrats will "not give a dime" to what he called the administration's "violent mass deportation machine." He said he hopes to secure one more signature, ideally from a Republican, on a discharge petition to force a vote on the American Dream and Promise Act, which would provide permanent status and a path to citizenship for Dreamers and recipients of Temporary Protected Status. He also said he is a "hard yes" on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The Government Accountability Office reported that the F-35 Joint Program Office cannot reliably track thousands of spare parts undergoing maintenance or repair, according to Breaking Defense. As of March 2026, more than 17,000 parts, worth an estimated $1.3 billion, were missing from the program's inventory system. Officials told GAO the value could be as high as $2.5 billion when missing cost information and other acquisition expenses are counted.

GAO said the gaps stem partly from incomplete contractor records that are not routinely integrated into the inventory system. The Enterprise Logistics Management System cannot interface with property systems run by Lockheed Martin and Pratt & Whitney, an issue GAO first reported in 2022 and said persisted as of August 2026. Contractor submissions for the joint spare parts pool arrive quarterly, so some records can be more than three months old. A December 2025 submission included serial numbers for only 29 percent of records and National Stock Numbers for 43 percent, and some records listed costs of one cent or less, which GAO said indicated possible data errors.

Since fiscal 2020 the office has spent at least $17 million on inventories, but GAO found its latest effort did not fully verify that parts were physically in place. In 2023, GAO found a prime contractor had lost more than 1 million parts worth over $85 million between May 2018 and October 2022.

GAO warned that inaccurate records could affect readiness and complicate the Pentagon's $13.7 billion Global Support Solution Reset strategy. It recommended stronger oversight of reported parts losses and clearer procedures, training and responsibilities. The Pentagon agreed with all four recommendations. A program office spokesperson said it is "actively working" on the issues and is establishing direct, real-time data interfaces between government and contractor systems. Lockheed Martin did not immediately respond to requests for comment. GAO did not link its findings to a separate Pentagon investigation into F-35 components shipped from Australia that ended up in Hong Kong.

Neros Technologies, a California drone maker, received a $450 million conditional loan from the Defense Department to expand domestic manufacturing of small drone components, according to Defense News. The loan came from the department's Office of Strategic Capital. Neros said it will commit another $165 million, bringing the total investment to $615 million. The company is described as a frontrunner in the Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program, a competition to find the best quality, most affordable small combat drone.

Ross Pederson, Neros' head of growth, said about 99 percent of small drones are made in China, which he called an untenable position for the United States. David Lorch, the office's director, said Neros has already shown it can design, manufacture and deliver small unmanned aircraft systems. He said the investment will boost its ability to make drones and components. Drone maker PDW received an $820 million loan from the office in July.

Before the loan, Neros did not make its own components; it contracted other firms and assembled the drones. Pederson said it has expanded in-house motor production and will soon make surface-mount technology components used on circuit boards. He said that by late next year roughly 80 percent of a drone's value should be made in-house.

Pederson declined to give the loan's interest rate or repayment timeline, but said it is not subject to forgiveness and that the department has set manufacturing goals centered on making components in the United States and offering them to the wider market.

The article also notes federal steps to build the domestic industry, including competitions and tariffs on imported drone components. Industry figure Brett Velicovich praised the tariffs. Pederson said the Pentagon's long-standing ban on buying Chinese electronics, rather than tariffs, drives military sourcing.

Two robotics announcements were reported by The Robot Report. At the Conference on Robot Learning in Austin, Texas, NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2, an updated open world action model, and Isaac Lab 3.0, a new version of its open-source robot learning framework. Separately, Boston Dynamics released a video of its Atlas humanoid moving on wheels as a research experiment.

NVIDIA said GR00T 2 was trained on diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of open-source egocentric data. It said the model completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations, and reached 71 percent average success across 50 tasks with one demonstration per task and 95 percent with five. NVIDIA claims it ranks among the top three models on several benchmarks. Isaac Lab 3.0 adds tighter integration with the Newton physics engine, which NVIDIA said lets it model cables and cloth, and reportedly delivers up to 2.5 times the training throughput of version 2.3 in one benchmark. Companies including Foxconn, Siemens and Nexuni are testing or evaluating GR00T 2.

The report noted NVIDIA's board opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang after he acknowledged a relationship with a business executive whom U.S. intelligence determined to be a Chinese spy. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

In the Boston Dynamics video, controls engineer Andy Wu explained that a custom adapter mounts an off-the-shelf scooter rim to Atlas' ankle actuator. The robot combined classical motor control with whole-body reinforcement learning, trained in simulation. The company said a wheeled Atlas is a research testbed, not a product. Wu's next question is how the system responds to failed actuators.

James Gunn and Peter Safran are leaving their roles as heads of DC Studios and will be replaced by Jeremy Latcham, a former Marvel executive, according to reports from Deadline cited by The Verge and Ars Technica. Latcham takes over on December 1 and will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

The change follows the closing of the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, which produced a combined Skydance company led by CEO David Ellison. Ars Technica said it has been barely two months since the merger. It said it is unclear whether Gunn and Safran chose to leave or were forced out, and that it is unclear what happens to their planned slate beyond Superman: Man of Tomorrow, which is in post-production. Gunn and Safran, who became co-CEOs in 2022, previously reported directly to Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav.

Gunn and Safran will continue to produce on various DC projects, including Man of Tomorrow, according to Deadline. In a joint statement they said they were proud of the team and eager to see the perspective Latcham brings. On Instagram, Gunn said the job was trying, that he disliked its at-times corporate nature and that he is relieved to return to filmmaking. He said he and Safran have just been engaged on another DC project he is writing.

Goldberg and Greenstein said Latcham brings deep reverence for DC and its fans. Latcham, a producer on films including Guardians of the Galaxy, Iron Man and The Avengers, said he is honored to lead DC Studios into its next era.

A sand bank overlooking a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah in Gaza collapsed on Sunday after high winds and heavy rain, killing five people and crushing at least three tents, according to The Guardian. Among the dead were an eight-year-old, a six-year-old and their mother. Their father survived because he was outside the tent.

Witnesses described a frantic rescue. Abdul Karim al-Sahhar said people dug through sand and that young men had to break up a huge boulder to reach those buried. Another witness, Abu Darbali, told Reuters the collapse sounded like an explosion. Video on social media showed people using hammers and shovels and searching by flashlight.

The United Nations said more than 26,000 households reported damage to shelters or belongings after the weekend's rainstorms. A Unicef spokesperson, Toby Fricker, said the collapse was waiting to happen because Gaza is extremely overcrowded. The Hamas-run government media office said about 70,000 tents were flooded on the first day of rain and that dozens of cracked walls and roofs collapsed.

Most of Gaza's 2.3 million people live in tents or ruined buildings. A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for eventual reconstruction, but little progress has been made, and negotiators have not agreed on terms for Hamas to disarm or Israel to withdraw troops. Israel says no reconstruction can happen before Hamas is disarmed.

A Gaza City council member, Mustafa Qazzaat, said Israel has not allowed prefabricated homes and has permitted only limited numbers of tents. Cogat, the Israeli defense ministry body overseeing aid, said more than 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks of tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothing have reached Gaza, along with fuel convoys for pumping facilities.

The White House on Monday did not rule out working with Democrats on a deal for immigrants who have lived in the United States illegally for more than a decade, according to Fox News. President Donald Trump raised the idea in his first sit-down interview since the Republican midterm losses, aired Sunday on "60 Minutes". Republicans are set to lose control of Congress in January.

Asked by host Ross Douthat about working with Democrats on immigration, Trump said he would love to do something and that enforcement had both helped and hurt him. He said he deserved an A+ for closing the border but that removing people with good jobs who committed one violation, entering illegally, was hurting him. He signaled willingness to work a deal for people in the country 10 or 15 years who have committed no other crimes. The White House would not say what such a deal could include.

A White House official told Fox News Digital that Trump never said the word amnesty and that the administration wants Democrats to show their cards. The official said more than 3 million people in the country illegally have left and called the border the most secure in history. Fox noted the interview was taped before Stephen Miller was named chief of staff.

Reaction was split. Representative Maria Salazar, a Florida Republican, said Trump's description matched her Dignity Act, which would offer legal status to people continuously present since 2020 who pay restitution and back taxes. Commentator Steve Cortes and others on X said an amnesty deal would be a betrayal. Democrats' response was not reported in the Fox article.
